After a while, midnight rang out from Westminster's tall tower. Each deep stroke of the bell seemed to send a shiver through the night. Then the railway lights went dark, leaving a single lamp shining like a huge ruby on a towering mast, and the city's roar began to fade.

At two he rose and wandered toward Blackfriars. Everything seemed unreal, like some strange dream. The houses across the river looked as though they were made of darkness. It was as if the whole world had been created again from silver and shadow. The great dome of St. Paul's rose like a bubble in the dim air.

Near Cleopatra's Needle, he noticed a man leaning over the stone railing. As he drew closer, the man raised his head, and the gaslight shone directly on his face.

It was Mr. Podgers, the palm reader! There was no mistaking that fat, sagging face, those gold-rimmed glasses, that weak, sickly smile, and that sensuous mouth.

Lord Arthur stopped. A brilliant thought struck him, and he crept quietly up behind the man. In an instant he grabbed Mr. Podgers by the legs and threw him into the Thames. A crude curse rang out, followed by a heavy splash; then everything was quiet. Lord Arthur peered anxiously over the railing. All he could see of the palm reader was a tall hat spinning in a swirl of moonlit water. Soon that sank too, leaving no visible sign of Mr. Podgers. Once he thought he saw the man's large, awkward body swimming toward the steps beside the bridge, and a dreadful fear of failure swept over him. But it was only a reflection, which disappeared when the moon emerged from behind a cloud. At last, it seemed, he had carried out what destiny demanded. He gave a deep sigh of relief and spoke Sybil's name.

“Have you dropped something, sir?” a voice suddenly asked behind him.

He turned and saw a policeman carrying a lantern with a round, focused beam.

“Nothing important, sergeant,” he replied with a smile. He called to a passing horse-drawn cab, climbed in, and asked the driver to take him to Belgrave Square.

For several days he swung between hope and fear. Sometimes he almost expected Mr. Podgers to enter the room. At other moments he felt that Fate could never treat him so unfairly. Twice he visited the palm reader's address in West Moon Street, but he could not bring himself to ring. He desperately wanted to know for certain, yet feared knowing.

At last the answer came. He was having tea in his club's smoking room, listening with some weariness to Surbiton's description of the latest comic song at the Gaiety, when the waiter brought in the evening newspapers.

The wavering gas-lamps curved away in a long line into the distance, and a lone hansom waited outside a small house enclosed by walls, its driver sleeping within. He hurried towards Portland Place, glancing back from time to time as if afraid someone followed him. Two men stood at the corner of Rich Street, studying a little notice pasted on a hoarding. A peculiar curiosity moved him to cross the road. As he approached, his eye caught the word “Murder” in black print. He gave a start, and his cheek reddened deeply. The notice promised a reward for information that would secure the capture of a man of middling height, aged between thirty and forty, dressed in a billy-cock hat, black coat, and checked trousers, with a scar on his right cheek. Again and again he read it, wondering whether the unhappy fellow would be taken, and how he had received that scar. Perhaps one day his own name would appear on placards along the walls of London. Perhaps a reward would one day be offered for him as well.

He felt sick with terror at the thought. Wheeling round, he hastened onward through the night.

He scarcely knew where his steps led him. He remembered vaguely straying through a maze of shabby houses, losing himself in an enormous net of gloomy streets; daylight was already bright when at last he emerged in Piccadilly Circus. Walking home towards Belgrave Square, he encountered the heavy waggons bound for Covent Garden. Their carters in white smocks, with cheerful weather-browned faces and rough curling hair, marched stoutly beside them, snapping their whips and occasionally shouting to one another. A plump little boy rode a great grey horse at the head of a jingling team, primroses tucked in his battered hat, his small hands clinging firmly to its mane as he laughed. Against the morning sky the towering loads of vegetables resembled heaps of jade, green jade set against the pink petals of a wonderful rose. Lord Arthur found himself strangely moved, without understanding why. To him the tender beauty of dawn held something unspeakably sorrowful, and he considered all the days that open in loveliness and close in tempest. These country folk, too, with their gruff, merry voices and careless bearing—how curious a London lay before their eyes! A London without the night's wickedness or the day's smoke, a pale spectral city, a lonely city of graves! He wondered what they made of it, and whether they knew anything of its magnificence and disgrace, its fierce pleasures coloured like flame, its dreadful hunger, and everything it fashions and ruins between morning and evening.

As they shouted these things, many of the women worked themselves into a blind fury. They spun around, hitting and clawing at their own friends until they fainted from the violence of their feelings. Only the men with them kept them from being trampled.

Even so, they wasted no time; not a moment! Foulon was at the Hotel de Ville, and someone might release him. Never, if Saint Antoine remembered his own suffering, humiliation, and injuries! Armed men and women poured from the neighborhood so quickly, sweeping even these last stragglers along with them, that in fifteen minutes Saint Antoine held no living person except a few old women and crying children.

No. By then they were all crowding the Hall of Examination, where the ugly, wicked old man was being held, and spilling into the open ground and streets around it. Monsieur and Madame Defarge, The Vengeance, and Jacques Three were at the front of the crowd, inside the Hall and quite close to him.

“Look!” Madame cried, pointing her knife. “Look at the old scoundrel tied up with ropes. What a fine idea, tying a bundle of grass to his back. Ha, ha! A fine idea. Let him eat it now!” She tucked her knife under her arm and applauded as though watching a play.

The people just behind Madame Defarge told those behind them why she was pleased. Those people passed the explanation to others, and those to still more, until applause echoed through the nearby streets. In the same way, over the next two or three hours of slow speeches and endless empty words, her frequent outbursts of impatience spread through the distant crowd with astonishing speed. The messages travelled especially easily because some remarkably agile men had climbed the outside of the building to watch through the windows. They knew Madame Defarge well and relayed her signals to the people outside.

Finally the sun climbed high enough to send a gentle beam directly onto the old prisoner's head, as though offering hope or protection. This kindness was more than the crowd could bear. In a moment, the flimsy barrier of dust and chaff that had held them back for a surprisingly long time scattered in the wind, and Saint Antoine had seized him!

The news instantly reached the farthest edges of the crowd. Defarge had only just leaped over a railing and a table to clasp the miserable man in a deadly grip. Madame Defarge had only just followed and wound one of the ropes binding him around her hand. The Vengeance and Jacques Three had not yet reached them, and the men at the windows had yet to swoop into the Hall like hunting birds dropping from high perches. Already the cry seemed to rise across the whole city: “Bring him out!
